inlines.text: Anthropic 的数学家 Levent Alpöge 周五表示，他用一个大语言模型解决了数学界最著名的未解难题。

blocks.text: 据 Scientific American 等美国媒体报道，Alpöge 在自己的网站上发布了一篇论文和配套的计算机代码。他在公告中写道：“我相信，在与 Claude 的合作下，我发现了黎曼猜想的证明。”

blocks.text: 从大学时代起，Alpöge 就把这个问题当作一个秘而不宣的终身目标，原以为要花上几十年。过去几个月里，他与 Anthropic 的 AI 模型紧密合作，负责把握方向，并在一个简化的玩具模型上把两种方法结合起来。等到转向真正的问题时，AI 接手了工作，在临近终点时把他远远甩在了后面。

blocks.text: 为了攻克这道难题，两人扩展了数学家 Stepanov 的一个思路——后者曾在另一个数学体系中解决过类似问题。该方法依赖的工具类似于高中数学里对光滑曲线求导，而这一招用在整数上通常行不通，因为单个数值无法像连续曲线那样求导。

blocks.text: Alpöge 和 Claude 绕开了这个障碍：他们把特殊的数学变换像链条一样串联起来，模拟出求导的效果。关键洞见由语言模型给出——它发现，对于一个长度为 X 的数列，需要串联的变换数量恰好是 X 的平方根。Alpöge 说，单是这类想法就足以让同行数学家震惊。

blocks.text: 黎曼 1859 年的假设试图在素数中寻找隐藏的秩序

inlines.text: 黎曼 1859 年的假设试图在素数中寻找隐藏的秩序

blocks.text: 记者 约瑟夫·豪利特在《科学美国人》的一篇详细分析中梳理了问题的核心。自伯恩哈德·黎曼于 1859 年提出这一假设以来，它一直是数论领域的北极星。大卫·希尔伯特将其列入 1900 年数学最重要问题清单，自 2000 年起，它作为克雷数学研究所七个“千禧年大奖难题”之一，悬赏 100 万美元。

inlines.text: 记者
约瑟夫·豪利特
在《科学美国人》的一篇详细分析中梳理了问题的核心。自伯恩哈德·黎曼于 1859 年提出这一假设以来，它一直是数论领域的北极星。大卫·希尔伯特将其列入 1900 年数学最重要问题清单，自 2000 年起，它作为克雷数学研究所七个“千禧年大奖难题”之一，悬赏 100 万美元。

blocks.text: 核心是像 2、3、5、7 和 17 这样的素数，它们只能被 1 和自身整除。它们堪称数学中不可分割的原子，因为其他所有整数都是素数的唯一乘积，比如 15 来自 3 乘以 5。斯坦福数学家布莱恩·康拉德将它们在数论中的地位比作物理学中的力。

inlines.text: 核心是像 2、3、5、7 和 17 这样的素数，它们只能被 1 和自身整除。它们堪称数学中不可分割的原子，因为其他所有整数都是素数的唯一乘积，比如 15 来自 3 乘以 5。斯坦福数学家布莱恩·康拉德将它们在数论中的地位比作物理学中的力。

blocks.text: 大约在公元前300年，欧几里得证明了素数有无穷多个，但它们在数轴上的具体位置看起来却像是随机的。随着数字变大，素数确实会变得越来越稀疏：0到100之间有25个素数，而1000到1100之间只有16个。18世纪末，还是少年的卡尔·弗里德里希·高斯利用长长的数表，找到了一个能粗略估算给定区间内素数个数的公式，但真实的素数总是不可预测地偏离这个估算值。

blocks.text: 高斯在哥廷根的学生黎曼，想找到一种方法精确计算这一误差，并 pinpoint 每一个素数。他的工具是黎曼ζ函数，它就像一台在带有横轴和纵轴的二维地图上运转的计算机器。给这台机器输入一个点的坐标，它就会输出一个新的数值。在某些点上，结果恰好为零。数学家把这些点称为零点。

blocks.text: 黎曼发现，这些零点解释了素数表面上的混乱。就像把一个音符分解成一个个单独的声波或泛音一样，零点修正了高斯的估算误差。每个零点就像管弦乐队中的一件乐器，它的垂直位置决定音高，水平位置决定音量。

blocks.text: 由于逐个计算无穷多个点是不可能的，黎曼在1859年猜想，所有关键的零点——即非平凡零点——都位于横坐标为二分之一的同一条垂直线上。罗格斯大学的亚历克斯·康托罗维奇解释说：“黎曼猜想说的是，素数管弦乐队中所有这些不同的乐器，都以完全相同的音量演奏。”表面上的随机性变成了严格的和谐。

blocks.text: 如果这两个证明中至少有一个成立，数论学家就能完全掌控素数在整个数轴上的分布。由于长期以来证明似乎遥不可及，数学家们已经提前研究了几十年。据康托罗维奇说，有数百篇论文假设黎曼猜想成立，而所有这些理论都将在一夜之间成为已确立的定理。由于阿尔珀格的AI方法和马苏洛的工作都覆盖了广义黎曼猜想，这一突破还将延伸到从简单方程到高维几何的各个领域。

blocks.text: 在这场突如其来的双重突破之前，该领域已经陷入僵局。除了马苏洛和康拉德这样低调的努力之外，几乎没有顶尖数学家直接研究这个问题，因为他们缺乏切入点。两年前，牛津大学的詹姆斯·梅纳德和麻省理工学院的拉里·古思证明，不可能有太多点远离黎曼线。尽管这是几十年来最大的进展，但在梅纳德本人和蒙特利尔大学的安德鲁·格兰维尔等同事看来，这只是一次小幅改进和权宜之计。

blocks.text: 即便 Masullo 的工作在这场正面交锋中保住了人类的尊严，像 Claude 这样的模型也已经变化得太快。仅仅一年时间，它们就从不可靠的工具，变成了能突破深层瓶颈、把数学界推入身份危机的系统。Alpöge 的心情很复杂：既为失去一颗指引了 150 年的北极星而伤感，又对接下来会发生什么抱有乐观。“但我在这一进展过程中看到的一切让我无比惊叹，我相信这是整个科学界迎来某种更伟大事物的一道曙光。”

blocks.text: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.

inlines.text: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.

blocks.text: Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," he wrote in his announcement.

blocks.text: According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well.

blocks.text: Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line.

blocks.text: To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line.

blocks.text: Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says.

inlines.text: Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof

blocks.text: Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement" on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

"hurried announcement"
on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

blocks.text: "It is all human, with no AI," Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said.

blocks.text: Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away.

blocks.text: About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)," Vakil wrote.

blocks.text: Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.

blocks.text: This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems. In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results. Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.

blocks.text: Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers

inlines.text: Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers

blocks.text: Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."

blocks.text: At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.

blocks.text: Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.

blocks.text: Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.

blocks.text: Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.

blocks.text: Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume," Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.

blocks.text: A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

inlines.text: A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

blocks.text: If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.

blocks.text: The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.

blocks.text: Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.

blocks.text: That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."

blocks.text: Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and push the math community into an identity crisis. Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."
